out and meet with the rating agencies. We have them review and we ask a number of questions

      Councilman Traficante, just prior to the meeting tonight, sat with the Finance Director.

blessing he would move through the bid process.

XIII. COUNCIL PRESIDENT COMMUNICATIONS

   •  Budget Process.

      Council President Wall stated that he placed this item on the docket for two
reasons. As we discuss the Budget process, he wanted to go over a few items that are
contained in the Charter that are apropo as we go forward in the budget process. He
asked the technical clerk to display a handout on the screen. He stated that Charter
Chapter 6 is where the budget is discussed. We are getting to the point where we are



2026-03-16/Rosalba/CouncilMinutes/2026/2026_04_20

partly through our hearings and starting to discuss what would happen regarding our
action on the Operating Budget. The Council has to act on the budget according to our
Charter by May 15th and he read Section 6.09 of the Charter. Our Appropriation
Ordinance requires a 7.45% increase. Knowing that, if we do not act or we voted it
down, it would go in as how the Mayor introduced it to us.  If we did not have enough
time and took no action at all, it would be the Mayor’s budget. Section 6.21 is where it is
worth discussing.  It states that “the City may not increase property tax levy cap by more
than 3%, but no higher than 4% above the amount levied for the previous FY unless
approved by an affirmative vote of at least a majority of the entire Council and at least
one of the conditions set forth in RIGL 44-5-2, which is outlined”, so one of those
conditions would have to be met to go to 4 and we would have to have at least the
majority vote. At that point it also states “furthermore, the City may not increase the
property tax levy by more than 4% above the amount levied in the previous FY unless
approved by affirmative vote of 4/5 of the entire City Council and at least one of the
conditions in the RIGL”. The way he reads that, it is 7 out of 9 Council Members. Those
two things coupled together create a problem. He does not know where we are at this
point, we are not quite done with that process, but as he states over and over, there is no
guarantee that we are going to pass that 7.4%.

      Councilman Ritz asked, if we vote yes and it is 7 out of 9 then we still need State
approval and then it would become the new tax increase? Solicitor stated that without
State authorization you can’t approve 7.5%. That is the first problem. As Council
President Wall stated, if you take no action, the Charter provision states that the Mayor’s
budget as submitted takes effect. The problem again, it is requesting a 7.45% increase,
again, can’t be done. That raises several possibilities, none of which are particularly
good and Mr. Strom could probably speak to it better than him. He can only state what
the legal options are and the legal options basically when it comes to budgets and when it
comes to a City or town that is in economic distress and the city or town is unable to, for
whatever reason, solve it internally, the only options at that point is to go to the Auditor
General, have them do a review. The Auditor General will not come in and run the City.
They may make suggestions, but it would still be up to this Council working with the
Administration to come up with a solution if you go down that road. The other nuclear
option would be a Central Falls scenario, a Providence School Department scenario or
Town of Johnston scenario back in the late 90’s where you contact the Auditor General
and tell them you cannot meet your obligations based on this budget that you have
currently and that probably begs the question of what happened. He thinks we are in
agreement that if the Council and Administration do not enact a budget going forward,
we would have to operate based on the prior year’s budget going forward, but that is a
temporary fix. Discretionary spending would have to be frozen and obviously
contractual obligations, payroll, pension contributions and things like that would still
have to be met, but there would probably be a freeze on all discretionary spending.
Worst possible case scenario would be appointment of an overseer as they did in Central
Falls, Johnston and Providence School Department. That is basically saying to the State,
sorry we are too far in the hole, we cannot meet our obligations. As to what Council
President Wall was talking about with Section 6.21 of the Charter, State Law does not
allow you to exceed 4% unless the General Assembly gives authorization or you go to the
Auditor General. You have to certify it, the Finance Director has to certify that one of
the conditions contained in the Statute have been met.  It is considered an emergency type
situation.  It has to be something that is genuinely an emergency and we can’t meet those
obligations. That scenario, if you can’t get General Assembly approval, what you do is
you go to the Auditor General.  If the Auditor General, and it is a big if, says ok I’ll let
you exceed it, it comes back in front of you and you are right back in the same position
because now you are going to have to vote whether or not to exceed that 4% and give
7.5%. Ultimately, it comes back into your lap whether you go to through the General
Assembly or go through the Auditor General. The nuclear option if you really can’t meet
your obligations and it is affecting some categories you mentioned, is State takeover.

      Councilman Ritz asked what happens if we go to the General Assembly and they
do not allow us to exceed the cap? Solicitor stated that it would have to go back to the
Mayor, but ultimately, it is going to end up in your lap. The one scenario that he is really
not certain on is what happens if none of those things work. Only thing he can think of is
at that point would be to get some type of clarification from the Court.  It might require a



2026-03-16/Rosalba/CouncilMinutes/2026/2026_04_20

Declaratory Judgement and put it in the hands of a Superior Court Judge because our
Charter does not go that far.

      Council Vice-President Haroian asked if you can go to the General Assembly
without this Council voting on a majority on a Resolution. Can the bill be submitted and
heard on the House floor if we did not pass the Resolution? Attorney Marcello stated that
the General Assembly could act without a Resolution of this Council. The reality is that
they will not act without a Resolution of this Council. They want the Mayor to support it
and they want the Legislative Body before they move on it.

      Councilman Traficante asked if the Mayor could go to the General Assembly
himself to try to ask for the 7.4%. Attorney Marcello stated that he could, they will not
pass it without a local Resolution, that is not a law, it is just a practice, policy that they
have. The problem is if you do not act by the 15th, the Mayor’s budget is a nullity
because it is above the 4% and he does not have authority to submit. His opinion, the
budget goes back to the Mayor and he has to submit a new budget within the Charter
provisions or 4%. There is a provision in the State Law, 45-2-3.2 that states “unless
otherwise provided by a city or town Charter, in an emergency caused by a failure of a
city or town to approve an annual appropriation measure, the same amounts appropriated
in the previous FY shall be available for each department and division thereof, subject to
a monthly or quarterly allotment in accordance with seasonal requirements as determined
by the city or town Chief Financial Officer, provided that expenditures for payment of
bonded indebtedness of the city or town and interest therein shall be such amount as may
be required regardless of whether or not an annual Appropriation Ordinance is enacted by
the City or Town Council”. So, first thing that would happen is we would revert to last
years budget, the last year’s rate, bond payment would have to be made no matter what it
is and that is the default initially while this whole thing plays out.

      Councilman Traficante stated that assuming worst case scenario and the City
Council does not come to an agreement, budget refers back, it goes to the Mayor, the
Mayor cannot exceed the 4%. The budget then becomes the previous year’s budget in the
interim, however, in the interim, since we passed Resolutions and Ordinances approving
contracts which exceed that amount, he asked what happens then? Attorney Marcello
stated that that is a good question, you do not have enough money to pay those
individuals. Whether that means temporary layoffs, bumping, job freeze, furlough days,
that is something that would have to be discussed and that is an Administration issue.

       Solicitor stated that the spread between what State Law allows and what our
Charter allows in terms of a tax increase versus what the Mayor says we need is a huge
spread. The difference between 7.5% and 3% is huge. There are mechanisms in place
under State Law if you find yourself in a genuine fiscal emergency. There are avenues
you can pursue, but they are not pleasant. You are going to forfeit control both the
Administration and the Council are going to forfeit considerable control so the longer this
goes on the more dire he thinks the situation becomes, the more you are going to be
looking at one of the options he outlined earlier.

      Council President Wall stated that the Council has sat through long hearings and
even if everything they complained about and even if everything they said was wrong and
need to be cut, they probably found less than $1 million in savings and only way they can
find savings is if they do bring people back to the table, some of the Unions back to the
table. The problem is the Council does not have authority to go to the Unions. They do
not know what is being done at this time and they are going to have an Executive Session
to discuss that matter.

      Councilman Buonanno stated that when the Director of Administration stood
before us a few meetings ago he said they saw this in August and here we are finding out
about it now.  If we knew about it in August, September, October and November it would
have given us some more time to contemplate this stuff as opposed to being under the
gun right now and that makes serving our constituents a lot more difficult.  If this Council
does not get to the seven votes to go over the 4% does that mean we fail to enact the
budget and the Mayor’s budget goes into effect and if the General Assembly approves
something more than that it goes into effect or does that mean he has to trim his budget to



2026-03-16/Rosalba/CouncilMinutes/2026/2026_04_20

4% tax increase and we go through it again? Solicitor stated that he and Attorney
Marcella discussed this the other day and the way the Charter provision is written is kind
of poorly drafted because the interpretation is that anything short of approval or anything
short of you amending it and voting to approve it is not adopting the budget and therefore
the Mayor’s budget as proposed would take effect, but the problem is we have a budget
based on a 7.5% tax levy which can’t happen legally. Councilman Buonanno stated that
the whole thing doesn’t make sense.  If we do not like a budget we vote it down it gets
enacted, correct? Solicitor stated that he thinks the intent was if you do not like it,
change it, that is why you have the power to amend. Rhetorically, if you can’t take the
time to sit and go through the budget and amend it to get to a place where you like it, well
too bad for you, the Mayor’s budget is going to rule the day. That is what he thinks the
intent was.

      Attorney Marcello stated that the Charter provision is designed to make sure that
the City always has an operating budget, so if the Council does not act, the Mayor’s
budget gets enacted and the Mayor has certain parameters within the Charter of how he
can go. The problem is the Mayor submitted a budget which is beyond those parameters
which needs General Assembly approval. He thinks both Solicitor and he agree that if
the Council fails to act or does not adopt anything short of adoption, we go back to the
Mayor’s budget, but the Mayor’s budget cannot be enacted because it is above the cap set
by State Law. In his opinion, the obligation then falls on the Administration to re-submit
a budget within the parameters that are allowed by Charter. Councilman Buonanno asked
if this means we start over again. Attorney Marcello stated that he believes you have the
ongoing provision that you are operating under. Solicitor stated that at some point,
someone has to submit a budget.

      Councilman Traficante stated that he would like to bring up a personal
experience, in the early 90’s the federal government eliminated a variety of federal funds
that were given to cities and towns, such as general revenue sharing, and they had a
situation where he had to go back to the Unions and had to ask permission to go back to
the Fire, Police, Laborers and School Department and had to sit down and renegotiate the
contracts with permission, so he could meet the budgetary expenses.  If push comes to
shove, we may have to do exactly that.

      Council President Wall stated that if he is not mistaken, once you renegotiate
that contract, it has to go before the members.

      Councilman Campopiano pointed out that if it does go beyond the deadline and
we have to go to the next session, it is going to compound the debt because we are still
working with last year’s. He asked if that is correct. Mr. Strom stated that if we did
revert back to this year’s budget we are currently in, there are holes in this year’s budget
which would be compounded again next year. Right now to get us to where we need to
be with the 7.5% proposal is about $15 million.  If you go to 4%, which is the cap, that is
8, you still have a shortfall of about $7 million and that is significant. You can go
through that budget and if you can come up with $7 million, you should be the Finance
Director because you are not going to find it. They have gone through every facet of the
budget.

      Council President Wall referred to Section 6.15 of the Charter and read into the
record. He stated that as he looks at this section, it states that each department, board,
commission, office, agency, except School Committee shall submit to the Mayor
requested allotments and appropriations for the entire FY quarterly. He asked where that
document would be and can members of the Council have that document for the next few
years so they can look at where they went off the run. Mr. Strom stated that when he was
Finance Director in the past, this was never done. Council President Wall stated that he
does not have the authority to direct the Finance Director to do it, but the Charter requires
it. Mr. Strom stated that he can provide information the Council President would like to
see but it is not from the department head, it is from our financial system. Council
President Wall stated that there seems to be a disconnect with our allocations and how
much we are spending. That is where a lot of our problems are. There is a frustration
that we are spending money, but there does not seem to be a mechanism to stop us from
spending money. Mr. Strom stated that he can provide a weekly or bi-weekly expense



2026-03-16/Rosalba/CouncilMinutes/2026/2026_04_20

accounts for each department and it will show which accounts are over budget and they
could give a light to that department head to explain why it is over budget.

      Councilwoman Graziano stated that she thinks what Council President Wall is
saying is you need to come up with a process to execute this specific section of the
Charter. We want to see this executed. Also, accountability, if the department is over the
first, the second and third time, when is it flagged and where is accountability? She
would like to know what process the Administration would like to set up and what
process the Council should set up. Mr. Strom stated that he believes that a few weeks
ago the Mayor sent communication to each department to not spend any additional
money unless it was totally essential or emergency.

      Councilman Traficante stated that all these problems could have been averted if
when developing a budget it became a more realistic budget that we do not have to
overestimate or revenues or underestimate our revenues. We should not be having these
kind of problems. He was surprised and taken aback that the Resolution he received to
extend the tax levy to 7.45% was submitted by a Representative that is outside of the City
of Cranston. Not one single Cranston Representative or Senator submitted that
Resolution. That tells him something.

III. PUBLIC HEARING FOR THE FISCAL YEAR 2026-2027 BUDGET


      Anthony Melillo, Vice-Chair of School Committee, 33 Harvard St., appeared to
speak and stated that he would like to start with a few of what he likes to call myths vs.
facts because public understanding matters when we talk about public schools. Myth #1,
during COVID, the School District added over 100 positions using federal funds. Fact, in
reality, over the last four years Cranston Public Schools has reduced their staff by 95
positions. This is the District making difficult decisions to live within its means. Myth
#2, the City of Cranston provides the School Department with millions of dollars every
year for their Operating Budget. Fact, over the last six years, the School Department has
received an average of approximately $1 million per year. While any support is
appreciated, that level of increase has not kept pace with the real costs we face, costs that
continue to rise every year. The heart of why they are here this evening is responsibility.
There are many challenges facing the Cranston Public Schools today. Their buildings are
aging, costs will be rising, mandates continue to increase, the financial pressure are real
and significant, but he would like to be clear about something, it is not the School’s fault
that many of the School buildings are crumbing with age.  It is not his fault that decades
of infrastructure needs have finally caught up with us, but it is their responsibility to fix
it.  It is not your fault that Federal and State mandates continue to grow every year.  It is
not his fault that healthcare costs continue to rise faster than revenues, but it is our fault,
our responsibility to manage them.  It is not your fault that ratified contractual obligations
must be honored.  It is not his fault that utility cost, transportation expenses and fleet
maintenance continues to climb, but again, it is our responsibility to address them. None
of us created these challenges alone. Many of these issues have developed over the years
even decades, but today we are the leaders entrusted with solving them and the truth is
responsibility does not belong to one body, one department, one Administration.  It
belongs to all of us, the School Committee, the City council, the Mayor’s Office and our
State partners. When we work together, Cranston succeeds because this is about 11,000
students who make up 11% of our City’s population, but6 100% of our future. Tonight,
he asks that we continue to work together and not assign blame for the past and accept
responsibility for the future.

      Kathrn Crowley, School Committee Member, appeared to speak and stated that
as a School Committee Member, she feels obligated to speak for the Schools and most
importantly for the children and the teachers of the City of Cranston. When the Mayor
spoke last night, he stated that the School Department had had a structural deficit for the
last four years. Simply put, it is the negative difference between what a City department
needs to function properly and the amount of Revenue available to finance those needs.
When the School District projects the expense to operate Schools for a year and the City
indicates it is only going to provide an amount less then needed to cover those expenses,
that creates a structural deficit. The Mayor’s proposal to increase the School District’s
budget by $1.5 million is inadequate to support the needs of this District this year. As a
taxpayer, she is very conscious of the tax raise. She also understands cost to taxpayers
for nearly everything they buy has gone up. The same cost increases are occurring itn eh
Schools. To maintain the same quality of education for our children, the Schools need
more funding. The School District is doing everything in its power to reduce its cost.
Studies are in place to reduce the number of Schools in the City within the next year or
two.

      Keith Catone, School Committee Member, 16 Windsor Rd., appeared to speak
and stated that to the extent that the City Budget is balanced at all, which of course we
realize now it is not, it has been balanced on the backs of the Schools because the Schools
are filling gaps that should otherwise be filled by the City. Last year, there were residents
in this Chamber who talked about and testified that they would be willing to pay more
taxes if it meant sustaining the high quality of our Schools. Collectively, our challenge is
how are we ensuring the public that we were going to be stewards, trustful stewards of
these dollars? We have to start being transparent and telling the truth. Claiming deficits
that are not there on the School side is not a good look. Claiming that a Budget includes
no layoffs when you know structurally that there will be and will continue to be layoffs as
a result of that proposed Budget on the School side.

Valerie Schule appeared to speak and stated that she listened to the Mayor’s
Budget presentation and found herself deeply troubled. She says to all government,
State, Federal and local, the days of going to taxpayers to dig yourself out of holes is
over. We have nothing left to give. Should you come to the taxpayers for more and
more, she wants to hear you did your part. Buying out some employees, though she is
thankful and happy for them, is not good enough. Unfortunately, the buck does literally
stop here. You will have to make painful tough decisions and the people expect you to
make them. One of the things she does love about Cranston is the Schools. They are
underbudget and you expect them to cut staff and programs. Mayor Hopkins told us what
this Budget did and did not do. She would like to tell what that $42 a month does for
many people, especially seniors. Our Budgets are already strained to the max. She
spends a lot of time going through grocery flyers, plan her meals according to the sales.
Movies are long since gone, eating out is a thing of the past, all she has left is breakfast
after Church and that may be on the chopping block if her taxes are going to go up. She
knows very few people who can afford this and many people it will hurt.

       Steve Stycos, 37 Ferncrest Ave., appeared to speak and stated that from 2024 to
this current Budget, the School funding has gone up 4.3% total for that period.
Meanwhile, the Fire Department has gone up 15.6% and the Police Department has gone
up 12.5%. Another big expense in the City Budget is Debt Service, payment of principal
and the interest and that is at an all-time high in this Budget of $12.5 million. When you
get to the Capital Budget, it is important that you cut those Capital projects that are not
essential. In the Audit that was done in 2025 Budget year, the Ice Rink has a cash
balance of $665,000. That has been set up as an Enterprise Fund and Director Strom,
who he has a lot of respect for, and he and Mr. Strom have disagreed that that should not
be in that. Why should the Ice Rink be in a separate Fund from the Park Department or
any other department? He does not think that has ever been approved by the City
Council.  If you look in the Audit, there is also a $852,000 cash balance in the Charter
School Account. That money says in the Audit it is restricted. He does not know why it
is restricted, but that would be something he would suggest be looked at especially
considering that the Charter School, as he understands it, is no longer independent, it is
part of the School Department. So, could they use that $852,000? Two other items that
should be looked at is tax breaks, which the Finance Committee has been discussing and
one of those is a tax break for Veterans. He pointed out that that tax break does not help
the Veterans who are most in need.  It should be income limited and there should be some
provision for people who rent. He also addressed the elderly tax break and stated that we
have a lot of people in this community who have enough money who are over 65. He is
eligible for that tax break, but he does not take it.

       Steve Frias, 107 Garden Hills Dr., appeared to speak and stated that he was
speaking in his personal capacity. He stated that last night he notified the Administration
that the Capital Budget for FY27 was incorrect. He hopes everyone has received the
correct copy today. The Charter and State Law both state that four fifths vote is required
to go over 4% tax levy so seven out of nine vote. The Charter requires the Budget be
adopted by May 15th. In the prior Resolution the City Council waived the April 1st
requirement. He does not believe you have the authority to do that. As far as the finance
problem the City is facing, based on his own view, this was a failure in local government,
failure by both City and Schools, Executive and Legislative and both parties. The failure
goes back to we were over relying on one-time revenue sources for the federal funds. He
warned about this in 2022 in writing and in person that if you do not get rid of the
reliance, you will end up with a structural deficit that you will have to end up paying for
or have multiple years of tax increase.  If the City had raised taxes by about 2-3% in 2021
or 2024, you would be at about a 2 or 3% increase now. He thinks that would be more
tolerable by taxpayers. Now you are at the stage of what to do. He does not recommend
going further above 8%. He thinks you need to look at spending cuts. People behind him
and for the rest of this week will be advocating for more money and do not want cuts. He
will be the voice of those that want spending cuts. Where do you cut? First, you have to
look at the Schools. He respects the School Department, but the problem he has is when
he looks at the Audit, which is an independent third party, they refer to the School
Department as having 1,554 jobs. That is FY2025 and they refer to an increase of

additional personnel staff post COVID19 pandemic. In FY2019, the Audit refers to them
as having full-time jobs of 1,530 so it looks like it is increased under the Audit. The
School Department can explain why the Audit says one thing and what they present to
you is another. In 2010, they had staff levels of between 1,431 to 1,462. When it comes
to the City funding more to the Schools, the State is not contributing enough. On the City
side, one department that has not had cuts is the Fire, it has gone up by 8 positions. you
probably have to eliminate 20 positions in the City to eliminate $6 million spending to go
to 4% levy.

      Council President Wall indicated to Mr. Frias that he handed out an amended
Capital Budget since there was an error in the initial one. He asked if that is correct and
that has been rectified. He asked Director Renzulli if that has been updated online.
Director Renzulli stated, yes.

     Anna Medeiros, School Committee Member, appeared to speak and stated that
she is present this evening as an advocate for all the students and the Schools asking for
all the financial support the Council can give or find to allow the Schools the opportunity
to do their jobs and to provide necessary services for the children in our community. To
her, it is really nice to have pickleball parks, beautiful parks if you are into that, but they
are truly nice to have.  It is not what comes to mind when she thinks of her pride of
Cranston especially when she knows the reality of where a majority of our students spend
their days and the environment that our teachers are expected to shape our children in.
she understands that in many ways the Council’s hands are tied, but please know that
every single dollar counts and urged everyone to do everything they can to help the
Schools get as close as possible to their ask so they can do right by the students and the
families that are counting on all of them.

      Domenic Fusco, Chair of School Committee, 167 Fiat Ave., appeared to speak
and stated that he is extremely proud of our School Committee. They have come together
and worked hard to make Cranston Schools the best they can be and thinks that they
have done a damn good job. For the past twenty years, he has stood before this
Committee as a parent, a School Committee Member and once again as Chair of the
School Committee and each year he has the same request. Do what you can to fund their
Budget. He thanked the most recent Councils for their support that they have given. The
additional funds they contributed have been a huge help. He deeply appreciates the
Mayor’s increase, however, it is not enough. Several years ago, it was a different story.
We had a Council that was adversarial towards the Schools. They said that the Schools
got more money from the State so they did not need to fund the Schools and all it did was
exasperate the problem. As everyone knows, the School Department is the largest
department in the City.  It employs under 1,200 workers now and maintains 20 buildings
and most importantly, they educate 11,000 students. The Schools do not generate any
funds. They must live with what was deemed appropriate by the City and State.  It is
easy to criticize and say you must live within your Budget.  If they had reliable funding
sources, maybe they could. This year, the Schools took a novel approach going through a
zero based Budget. During Budget hearings, one of his colleagues asked what percentage
of the Budget do we actually control, the answer is less than 10%. They tried to get
creative. They have ESSRA funds available, they used them, they got additional
programming, they used them to fill some positions, but unlike our neighbors to the
immediate South, they knew they had to start putting those positions back into their
Budget and they did or they eliminated them. This is why they are not int eh same
position as them. Most of our Budget goes towards salaries and benefits. Like the City,
they are grappling with rising healthcare costs. As a self-insured District, they have seen
medical claims spike turning a once healthy surplus into a deficit we must now repay.
Cranston Public Schools are truly the poster child of what? Doing more with less.
Cranston is the second largest School District. On average, they spend $19,950 per
student, well below State average of $22,800. Many other cities and towns are operating
closer to $25,000 per student and we are showing results. We are doing the job, we are
doing with less, but we can’t do it anymore.  It is time to do something. We have no
choice but close Schools, increase class size, cut programs. Something we do not want to
do.

Jonathan Francis, President of Local 1363, appeared to speak and stated that he
understands the City is hurting. He thinks everyone in this room wants to try to achieve
the same goal. The Police and Fire Departments have taken a beating in the newspapers
over their Overtime Budget. He would like to clear up a few misconceptions. A
comment was made this evening that the Fire Department has expanded by eight
positions without any vacancies. That is a half truth statement. The Fire Deparmtent has
expanded by eight spots. They put on a fifth rescue that is severely needed. Last time a
rescue was added was in 1984 and they are doing about 8,000 runs a year. This rescue
was added at the beginning of this yer and the City is doing currently 18,000 runs. That
is the true part. The false part is the vacancies. Currently, the City of Cranston, as of
tomorrow when the Chief of the Department retires, they are going to be down twelve
members. That may not seem a lot to some people who are not in the profession, but that
is additional shifts that they are required to work. On top of that, they are at the mercy of
the State Retirement Board when it comes to occupational injuries and illnesses, which
severely impacts their Overtime as well. They already operate at minimum manning.
Minimum manning is 43 firefighters per shift. The national standard is to have four
firefighters per truck. They currently fall short of that standard on half of the trucks in
this City. That leads to injuries at fire on the fire ground which increases that Overtime
Budget. Fire Department employees have been always willing to work with the City and
they always stand with everyone in the City. The misconception that they are driving up
the Overtime Budget is not true. There are some factors that do attribute it to it, however,
the mechanism for the Fire Department to reduce that number has been stripped from the
them over the last few years. The Fire Department stands with you and willing to work
with the Council.

       Director Renzulli stated that the Traffic Engineer did show her a file dating back

XIII. COUNCIL PRESIDENT COMMUNICATIONS

   • DE LA COMUNIDAD CHARTER SCHOOL AND LEGAL COMPLAINT
     FILED

      Council President Wall stated that approximately two weeks ago, a complaint
was filed in Superior Court by the City of Cranston and the City of Pawtucket against the
De La Comunidad Charter School and RIDE for their passage, as we and Pawtucket
believe that it was passed in according to the Ordinance that would classify it as a
Network Charter, which includes both Elementary and Secondary Schools. Such a
Charter would require the City Council of said City, said City, ourselves and Pawtucket
along with Providence to have filed a Resolution approving them a Resolution, they did
not ask us for a Resolution.  It is their contention that they are not a Network Charter so
we filed a complaint. We have not head back from Superior Court yet. Solicitor Millea
and Amanda Cascione from the School Committee worked on it on behalf of the City of
Cranston and it was a similar situation in Pawtucket. We are on the same lawsuit and he
asked Attorney Marcello to speak on it.

      Attorney Marcello stated that he spoke to Solicitor Millea today and the case has
been filed in a timely manner. We are waiting for a Summons to be generated by the
Superior Court. Once the Summons is filed in the Court, then we need to serve the
complaint on the RI Department of Education and the City of Providence as a Defendant
because they are the interested parties in this obviously. From that, there will be a whole
schedule. Basically, we are asking the Court to look at the Statute that establishes this
and whether or not RIDE violated the Statute or they did not, meaning did they get the
proper Resolution to approve this.  It is not going to happen overnight, but it is a process
that is going to be followed and he believes that because Pawtucket is in the same
position that the City is in, he believes that Solicitor Millea is indicating that he will be
working with that City Solicitor as well to move the case forward. Other than that, there
is not much for the Council to do other than wait for the Judge’s ruling.

      Council President Wall stated that this item is listed on the docket for
informational purposes and as more information comes out, we will pass it on to
everyone. We are a Country of laws and regardless of how you feel about a Charter
School, in his view and many of the Attorneys he has spoken to, this position as it holds,
will save our City when it comes to fruition, annually $2 million each year until that
Charter School decides it wants to expand itself and then it will cost us more than $2
million a year and given our current situation, that is a pretty heavy number and that is
why he put this item on the docket and he will certainly keep everyone posted on the
success.

      Councilman Buonanno thanked Council President Wall for taking the lead on
this. He agrees wholeheartedly and thanked Council President Wall for doing the right
thing for the City. Whether or not we agree or disagree with what the Charter School
stands for or what they are going to do, you have to follow the rules. To him, it is a clear
shirking of the rules. Not only is it a slap to our face or Pawtucket’s face, it is basically
them saying that they do not need the Council’s approval, yes they do and he hopes this
goes well for us.

      Councilman Traficante stated that what bothers him is this is not like RIDE
overlooking the rules set in place for Charters. When we established a Charter in
Cranston back in 2002, we had to get approval by the School Committee, had to get
approval by the City Council, even the Mayor had to give his approval. We had to get
approval by the Cranston Teachers Alliance. There is a procedure to follow. He is
disappointed that RIDE will allow that to slip.

      Council President Wall stated that he is still waiting on Providence and
Providence did not give a Resolution of approval either, but they did not join on our
complaint to Superior Court. He has reached out to Providence and spoke to the
President of the School Board this afternoon and he was very surprised that the Council
had not filed a complaint because Providence is also in a precarious financial situation.

   •  DISCUSSION, RECEIPT AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT OF
    CORRESPONDENCE DATED FEBRUARY 5, 2026 FROM R.I. AUDITOR
    GENERAL CONCERNING CITY OF CRANSTON FY2025 AUDIT REPORT
    AND MUNICIPAL AND SCHOOL DEFICITS

      Councilman Andujar stated that there will be a special Council meeting on
February 23, 2026 at 6:30 p.m. regarding the Audit.

      Council President Wall stated that he put this item on the docket because he
thinks we should have a discussion going forward. This letter from the Auditor General
seems to have been sent to just about everyone in the State outside of us as well. He
asked if Mr. Igoe would like to address this letter.

      Mr. Igoe stated that he put together a packet because he spoke to the Auditor
General today and the printed version of the Audit is not available yet.  It is on its way
here by FedEx. The Auditor indicated to him that he spoke to the Council President and
Councilman Andujar and there is a meeting scheduled for Monday evening to have them
give their presentation. He has printed copies of what he thinks was relevant and if there
are any questions, he will be available to answer them. He indicated that the actual Audit
is on the website.

      Council President Wall stated that as to the letter, certainly, we are concerned
with the numbers that come through. Considering our General Fund end of FY resulting
in an operational deficit of $6.5 million. The Schools Unrestricted Fund, a deficit of $3.9
million. This is not a finger pointing moment.  It is a moment where we have to say
“what happened”? “How did we get here”? “What are we going to do to fix this”? and
“What are we going to do to fix this so it does not happen again”? He is sure that that is
the position of the Administration as well, but he thinks we may have to look at some of
these things as well. The second page of the letter discusses the RIGL 45.12.2.2 and it
states the City did not submit completed budget to the actual report during the FY25. He
asked if that is true. Mr. Igoe stated that it is true, we did not submit it, but we do post it
every month and he sends it out electronically every month to the Council and to the
rating agencies and the Administration.

      Council President Wall asked if the monthly reports he receives, was the City
supposed to send it to the Auditor General’s Office as well? Is this something we have
not been doing in the past? Mr. Igoe stated that we used to send it to them all the time
and then when COVID happened, that changed the report and it was kind of laxed off and
then we received the second letter that is in the attachment on March 3rd of last year
saying that they were going to start back up in FY26, which started July of last year. The
first report due to them was now in January and he forwarded the report that is on our
website to the Auditor General and to the Department of Revenue. Council President
Wall asked if we are back on track with that matter, and if we are, it’s good to hear.
Also, in the letter, they discuss encouraging the City and School Officials to consider
implementing budgetary and spending controls for the remainder of the FY2026 to
minimize any potential operating deficit for the FY ending June 30, 2026. He assumes
the City must be having meetings regarding this. Mr. Igoe stated, yes, they are, for the
last month or two. Council President Wall stated that he thinks it would be important for
the Council to be updated on this matter. As we go forth, maybe during the Finance
Committee meetings this update can be given. The next Finance Committee meeting will
be March 2nd. There was a meeting on January 28th with the School Department and the
City and he asked Mr. Igoe to tell the Council substance of that. Mr. Igoe stated that

basically, it is summarized in the letter.  It was a conference call with the Auditor
General, Department of Revenue, School Department and City Administration and once
the Auditor General had received our Audit report for last year, the year ending June 30,

the Finance Committee agenda.

      Councilman Andujar stated that he is very concerned with this letter even on

we need to be seated at the table to see what is going on over there. Attorney Marcello

      Councilman Traficante asked if the Administration know or did not know that

Every one of those financial statements in front of them that they could have monitored

appropriately and he, himself, admitted that during the period of negotiations of three

      Council Vice-President Haroian asked Director Moretti when he was made

XIII. COUNCIL PRESIDENT COMMUNICATIONS

   •  Da la Comunidad Charter School, letter to RIDE regarding concerns with
       approval

      Council President Wall stated that he sent a letter to RIDE approximately a
week ago regarding the Da la Comunidad Charter School and although it is not necessary
to read the entire letter, the substance of it was that Da la Comunidad did not get the
required Resolution or Ordinance approving of their Charter School to be a sending City.
He read the letter into the record and stated that besides RIDE, it was also sent to the
members of the Department of Education and members of the City Council. He did get a
response a number of days later and basically their attorney stated that the law did not
apply because Da la Comunidad is not looking to have more than one school.  It does
state in the law that a Charter School that does encompass an elementary and a secondary
school would be considered a network Charter School.  It seems to be a bit of
gamesmanship or semantics as they said it was not plural. In his view, and some of the
attorneys have said that a K-12 School absolutely encompasses an elementary and a
secondary school. The other sending cities were Pawtucket and Providence. They have
also sent letters subsequently and he will keep everyone posted as to what happens, but as
of right now, we are in touch with our School Committee and some of the attorneys here.





U/Rosalba/CouncilMinutes/2026/2026_01_20

He has also been in touch with Senator Hanna Gallo, who is the author of the law and she
concurs that it seems like De la Comunidad Charter School is trying to circumvent the
law in this respect. He questioned why a school that seeks and who claims to be so in
tuned with helping the citizens of the City of Cranston, not even consider getting the
consent of this elected officials, he means the City Council, the School Committee, the
Mayor, the Superintendent who is appointed by the School Committee and also the
President of the Teachers Union. They did not get the support, they did not ask for the
support of one of those bodies. To him, that seems like something is wrong. He will
keep everyone updated on this matter.

      Councilman Traficante stated that he agrees with everything Council President
Wall stated and also stated that he is Chairman of the Charter School in Cranston and
before they got their Charter, they had to get permission of the Council. They had to get
permission of the Cranston School Committee and on top of that, they became a subset of
the Cranston School Department. The Cranston School Department holds what is called
the LEA, Learning Education Agency, for the Charter School in Cranston so they did
none of that.

      Councilman Ritz stated that he appreciates Council President Wall sending the
letter and he shares the same concerns. As everyone knows, it has an impact on School
funding and classroom resources.

      Councilman Buonanno thanked Council President Wall for sending that letter
and stated that many of us were present at the public meeting held at the Cranston Public
Library and for those that were there, the elected officials in the room had a lot of
questions. There definitely was not a ringing positive endorsement from any of our
elected officials. He has tremendous amount of faith in our public schools and Cranston
Public Schools is second to none and he has tremendous amount of faith in our
Superintendent and School Committee to give the education that Cranston needs. He
hopes that the leaders of the School Committee will confer with their legal counsel and
perhaps take it a step further based on the interpretation of the law that was heard.

      Council Vice-President Haroian thanked Council President Wall for what he
has done. As everyone knows, this has a big financial impact on the budget, on the
Cranston School Department and on the City budget. She believes it is about $19,000 per
student that the City loses in State funding per child that goes to a Charter School and
that makes a big difference with 200 students. You are talking hundreds and millions of
dollars. We offer all these things in our public schools.

      Councilman Andujar stated that he is a strong believer in education and most of
these kids that are probably going to go to Da la Comunidad are probably going to come
from Ward 3 so he is totally all for education, but he is not in agreement with them
bypassing this body. He applauded Council President Wall for sending that letter and
hopes he follows through with it and he will have his support if this come back to the
Council and even just to ask.

21    Duarte, Francisco del Rosario Sánchez, and Ramón Matías Mella continues to inspire Dominicans
22    at home and abroad; and
23
24  WHEREAS, the Dominican community in Cranston is a vibrant and essential part of the social,
25    cultural, civic, and economic fabric of the city, numbering an estimated approximately 5,300
26   Dominican residents in Cranston, representing a meaningful share of the local population; and
27    across Rhode Island, there are approximately 60,700 Dominican residents, reflecting the deep and
28   enduring ties between the Dominican Republic and the people of Rhode Island; and
29
30  WHEREAS, Dominican Americans and those of Dominican descent in Cranston and throughout
31   Rhode Island contribute to the richness of our community through entrepreneurship, arts and
32    culture, service in education and public safety, community leadership, family life, and the everyday
33    pursuits of civic participation and community building; and
34
35  WHEREAS, Dominican Independence Day provides an opportunity for all residents to celebrate
36   Dominican heritage, reflect on the history of the Dominican Republic, honor the achievements of
37   Dominican Americans, and reaffirm our shared commitment to diversity, inclusion, and mutual
38    respect;
39
40  NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT, the Honorable Cranston City Council
41
42        1.  Hereby recognizes and honors February 27 as Dominican Independence Day in the City
43           of Cranston.
44        2.  Celebrates the many contributions of Dominican residents and Dominican Americans, both
45            in Cranston and across the State of Rhode Island, and acknowledges the positive impact of
46            their heritage, culture, and civic engagement on the life of this city.

51            to recognizing and honoring the diversity and cultural heritage of all its residents.
